what: The newsroom's article feed (articles/graphs.json) with each article's number (articles/ids.json), copied by site/build.py --refresh-articles so this site can link and curate them. Refresh it with the newsroom.

articles.title: Stop the bleeding, then ask for it back: a helper, an agent and a friendly letter for the subscriptions you keep and do not use
articles.teaser: A helper and an agent ask what you used, ask nicely for a pause and a refund, stop the payments either way, and publish what each company did.

articles.title: Who owns the words: agents can make decisions, but they cannot hold responsibility
articles.teaser: Agents in loops make real decisions, but responsibility stays with whoever granted the reach; disclosure is a label, not a team to manage.

articles.title: What open source is, and what it is not: six misconceptions, a little history, and why the point is that nobody can lock you in
articles.teaser: Open source is a copyright licence, not a free-for-all: six misconceptions corrected, and why the point is that nobody can lock you in.

articles.title: Not a straight line: working for RiskMandate by working on the newsroom, and why the thinking is never wasted
articles.teaser: Working on the newsroom solved RiskMandate's oldest problem in two days: progress is not a straight line, and the thinking is never wasted.

articles.title: Sovereignty is the ability to move: play where the ball is going, take away the dot, and keep a twin that works
articles.teaser: Sovereignty is the ability to move: take away each dot on the map, and keep a twin that works for the minimum viable company, tested in QA.

articles.title: The records ran out: a fresh agent found the shared contract in two MCP calls, and where sgit and RiskMandate fit at the edges
articles.teaser: A fresh agent found a shared contract in two MCP calls from build records; where the records stopped is exactly where evidence labels and sgit vaults fit.

articles.title: Move the cloud, not the code: twins, sovereignty that works in practice, and the migration that pays for itself on the day you switch
articles.teaser: Workloads stay on hyperscalers because moving means changing code; a twin lets the code not know, and the value in the twin is what signs the migration.

articles.title: Judo for small countries: where Portugal, Romania and Estonia can add the most value in AI, and why the race for GPUs is not it
articles.teaser: A small country should not race for GPUs: the opportunity is the plumbing its talent stands on, built once as open infrastructure, with small models.

articles.title: Why I love Wardley maps: the best of ours, how I read one, and a map inside a map inside a map
articles.teaser: The best of our Wardley maps with their context, why the technique matters, one map read as a story, and a map inside a map inside a map.

articles.title: Places of highest leverage: where to focus when the agents can go in every direction, told with three days of real steps
articles.teaser: Where to focus when agents can go in every direction: the place of highest leverage, shown on three days of real steps, two walked back and one parked.

articles.title: Agentic cost is an engineering problem: a business plan for a service that reads the logs a company already has and finds the money, then the engineering
articles.teaser: A business plan: read the logs a company already has, draw each agent's footprint, twin and policy, and find the money first and the engineering second.

articles.title: How the voice works: why these articles sound like me, with a section in which Claude explains it from its side
articles.teaser: Why these articles sound like their author: a corpus, the voice memos, seven wording rules and a reader who corrects, with Claude explaining it from its side.

articles.title: From a spreadsheet to a folder per person: how to run your contacts the way our agents do, with Google Drive, Gmail and the Claude app, before you touch a vault
articles.teaser: A walkthrough from a spreadsheet CRM to one Drive folder per person, worked by Claude under a six-line policy, with five exercises, before any vault is needed.

articles.title: The key is the billing system: VoiceDebrief, a product with no server, the one thing it cannot sell, and who could let it
articles.teaser: VoiceDebrief runs with no server on the user's own key; the one thing it cannot sell is a capped key, and this maps who could allow it and what to ask them.

articles.title: Ways to read one article: the finished piece stays at the centre, and the reader picks the way in
articles.teaser: The five readers' views arrived as folds inside the long piece; now the reader picks the way in, with a default, and the finished article stays at the centre.

articles.title: Firing journalists is the worst thing a publication can do: what a hiring decision says about where a publisher is going, and who to hire instead
articles.teaser: A hiring decision is a direction of travel: fire the journalists and the centre of gravity moves to packaging, where the metric makes clickbait by construction.

articles.title: The site is an inbox: deciding before reading, marks that build the reader's own graph, and why I could not write this brief until the vault existed
articles.teaser: The site as an inbox that starts empty: decide fast before reading, mark slowly while reading, build a graph you own, and sign what you send to the newsroom.

articles.title: The vault is live: from a design on 11 October to a reader's vault on newsroom.sgit.ai by two in the morning, and how all of it fits together
articles.teaser: The reader's vault runs on newsroom.sgit.ai: a passkey opens three real vaults, each device writes one file, and the architecture is drawn as it stands.

articles.title: Two agents, one vault: the Industry Wire is written into an encrypted vault by one agent and drawn by newsroom.sgit.ai, which holds only the read key
articles.teaser: One agent writes the Industry Wire into an encrypted vault; newsroom.sgit.ai holds only the read key and draws it, so a commit reaches the page with no release.

articles.title: The article remains a product: Jonathan Palmer's four outputs for a newsroom with no human readers, checked against one that runs
articles.teaser: Jonathan Palmer's four outputs for a newsroom with no human readers, quoted line by line and checked against newsroom.sgit.ai as it runs, screenshots included.

articles.title: Go slow to go fast: moving the newsroom from an explorer project to a villager one, with the brief to do it
articles.teaser: The newsroom is live and charging. Move the reader code to its own repo, same bytes and same bugs, then map, test, review and refactor before new features.

articles.title: The passkey opens the vault: a door per path, a master vault for every user, and no server of ours
articles.teaser: Tested: a passkey's PRF bytes compute a door that holds the master's key, and a different path to the same passkey gives different bytes, so a door per path.

articles.title: I miss it, so it is working: the people who decide the roadmap have to use the product, and the vault the newsroom now needs
articles.teaser: I read the newsroom on four devices and they do not agree. Missing a feature is the best sign; the makers must use it. And the brief for the reader's vault.

articles.title: Brief the agent too: the people I talk to work with agents, so what I send has to reach both
articles.teaser: The people I advise read through agents. Content needs a second package, a brief for their agent, and memory, so it reads what changed, not everything.

articles.title: From me to you, in a link: a personal reading list, two briefs to build and use it, and the loop that makes it a day's work
articles.teaser: A reading list from one person to another, in a link the server never sees; a brief to build it, a brief to use it, and the loop that ships it in a day.

articles.title: A model in the tab: Chrome now ships an LLM to capable desktops, and it is the hardest piece of the client-side puzzle
articles.teaser: Chrome now ships a language model any page can prompt, offline, on capable desktops. The last piece of the client-side puzzle, with rough edges.

articles.title: No server, by design: first I retired the database, now I am retiring the back end
articles.teaser: First the database went, now the back end: the SGit Newsroom runs all its logic in the browser, on commodity servers that cannot read your data.

articles.title: The agent is the reader: why agents will pay for graphs, personas and signed claims, because it is cheaper than not paying
articles.teaser: Agents pay to read the raw web and guess its meaning. A curated graph answers for 90% fewer tokens, so paying the publisher is cheaper than not paying.

articles.title: Where the platform draws the line: Microsoft Execution Containers, the shared responsibility model for agents, and the business logic above it
articles.teaser: Microsoft's MXC and ACS, briefed field by field and mapped to Agent Behaviour Policies: the platform bounds what it can see; the business logic is above.

articles.title: The same argument, in our words: Satya Nadella on models as insider risks, translated into the language of RiskMandate
articles.teaser: Satya Nadella's case for treating models as insider risks, translated idea by idea into our vocabulary: reach, mandate, gap, barriers and accepted risk.

articles.title: Authority outside the model: an answer to Satya Nadella on models as insider risks, principle by principle, with what we run, what we ship and what we plan
articles.teaser: Satya Nadella's seven principles for models as insider risks, answered one by one: what we run, what is design, and the five things the list leaves out.

articles.title: How to run synthetic users on your own site: five people who do not exist, a browser, and an afternoon
articles.teaser: Five invented users, a model reading screenshots, and a real browser: how to run synthetic users, from three studies.

articles.title: A link to a persona: send people to the newsroom as someone, not as nobody
articles.teaser: Send a CISO to the newsroom as a CISO: personas kept in a vault by the newsroom's agents, opened from a link, followed or forked.

articles.title: Pay after you read: how a reading meter became a working business model in one afternoon, one release at a time
articles.teaser: Seven releases in one afternoon turned the reading meter into a working model: pay after you read, and the rating sets the price.

articles.title: Where the vault keys live: key management at sgit-ai v0.20.0, and what comes next
articles.teaser: Vault key management at sgit-ai v0.20.0: the one secret, where keys are kept, how they travel sealed on append lanes, and what comes next.

articles.title: The infographic bake-off: which image model for which job, judged blind on 10 October 2026
articles.teaser: Every image model on OpenRouter, eleven briefs, 101 images judged blind, $10.44: which model for which infographic, and what it costs.

articles.title: Pay to keep your persona: readers should pay because it helps them, not because they feel they should
articles.teaser: Readers should pay because it helps them: a persona with a name and a graph, several for focus, and one that follows you between devices.

articles.title: Who will game the reading meter? Eight kinds of reader, nine ways to cheat, and the risks that will actually happen
articles.teaser: Eight kinds of reader, none of them attackers, nine ways to cheat a browser meter, and the quieter risks that will actually happen.

articles.title: Going live with the reading meter: pay for what you read, go below zero if you like, and the numbers we will check in eight weeks
articles.teaser: Pay for the share of a page you read, go below zero with no nagging, top up £5 on Stripe: the plan, and the numbers we check in eight weeks.

articles.title: Open source is not free: who pays to keep the long tail working?
articles.teaser: An old iMac, the long tail of old versions that projects are not paid to support, measured from public data, and five ways to pay for it, simulated.

articles.title: One article, five readers: a librarian, a cartographer, a historian, an explainer and a storyteller read the same piece
articles.teaser: Write the article first, then send five agent readers through it: a catalogue, an ontology and maps, the arc, two minutes, and a deck.

articles.title: A meter in the browser: a penny a page, a history you keep, and a site that picks for you
articles.teaser: Every page now costs a few pence from £5 of credit kept in your browser, and the reading history it keeps is what personalises the site.

articles.title: Re-anchoring: keeping an agent's rules alive through every summary, and a canary that shows when they are not
articles.teaser: Summaries keep under 2% of a long session. Re-anchoring prints the agent's rules back after each one; a canary report shows it is working.

articles.title: A second reader the agent cannot skip: how two wrong emails became a gate on every draft
articles.teaser: Two emails went out in my voice despite a written rule. The fix: a hook that makes a second model approve every draft, failing closed.

articles.title: The AI governance stack, as a graph: an answer to Hari Kota, built
articles.teaser: Hari Kota's ten-layer AI governance stack, kept as posted and turned into a fractal semantic graph: the gaps become missing edges, and queries.

articles.title: RFC 0001: two ways to add public-key cryptography to sgit, and the questions we want you to answer
articles.teaser: A Request for Comments: two key pairs so a reader cannot write, sealed files only named people can open, and fourteen questions for reviewers.

articles.title: A Mac of the agent's own: a business plan for agent desktops, what Apple's licence allows, and three behaviour policies
articles.teaser: A business plan for a Mac of the agent's own: what Apple's licence allows, a desktop built from vaults per run, and three behaviour policies for one agent.

articles.title: Ten hard questions for RiskMandate, answered: the mandate, the reach, the gap, and what we are deliberately not
articles.teaser: Ten hard questions from a conference, answered in a two-hour interview: what RiskMandate does, what it deliberately is not, and how mature each part is.

articles.title: How I work with Claude: one session per topic, agents with names, and memory you curate
articles.teaser: A practical guide from a year of daily use: one Claude session per topic, named agents with a role.md, curated memory, vaults, and policy before connectors.

articles.title: The waiting room knew first: a live local story, and the gap where local information used to be
articles.teaser: Staff at two London hospitals said the IT was down; nothing a local could check showed it. A live local story about where local information comes from now.

articles.title: Encrypted memory for agents that run somewhere else: sgit deployment patterns, from a Mac mini to Kubernetes
articles.teaser: Agents in isolated, ephemeral places need memory that outlives them. Five sgit deployment patterns, from a Mac mini to Kubernetes, with ciphertext-only servers.

articles.title: Knowing when to stop: what experience gives people, and what we have to design into agents
articles.teaser: Knowing when to stop is the hard part for people and agents: what experience gives people, and the constraints that give agents the same perspective.

articles.title: Agency is not a yes: a scale for human and agent decisions, from rubber stamp to the reviewer who fixes the source
articles.teaser: A yes or no is not agency: seven dimensions, a seven-level scale for people and agents, and the review as a QA step that fixes the source.

articles.title: Hope or enforcement: one customer service agent, three designs, and who keeps each promise
articles.teaser: One customer service agent built three ways, each with an Agent Behaviour Policy: how much of each policy is hope, and what one run can reach.

articles.title: Who are you protecting against? Draw the security line where the attacker is, not above it
articles.teaser: Before deciding how secure to be, name the attacker: a six-tier ladder, an air-gapped Mac mini read against it, and eight startups drawing their line.

articles.title: Every mistake added a rule: complexity, agents, and the way back to shipping
articles.teaser: When every agent mistake adds a rule, complexity wins: map the process, move each piece right as a small shipped component, and keep the rigour for the work.

articles.title: Liquid content needs water: liquefy the journalist's notebook, not the finished product
articles.teaser: A reply to FT Strategies on liquid content: the water is the reporting, so liquefy the journalist's notebook, keep the writing theirs, and pay per use.

articles.title: The bridge, followed to the end: what one local story is worth when it is kept as a graph
articles.teaser: A bridge closure simulated on a story vault: newsworthy on 5 days, needed on 57, used by three readers, four buyers and an agent, and paid back to its sources.

articles.title: Story vault underneath, Reader Skills on top: why local journalism has the most to gain
articles.teaser: Markus Franz's Reader Skills on top, the story vault underneath: each skill is a graph query, and local stories can pay back down their chain of sources.

articles.title: Zoom into an agent's behaviour policy and you find the business logic
articles.teaser: Below the first rules, an agent's behaviour policy is the business: functions, processes, clients, values. Layered, owned, counted, and where vendors plug in.

articles.title: A locked-down desktop for an agent, by the minute, is still hard to rent
articles.teaser: Nine properties a safe agent desktop needs, nine products against them, the macOS day-long lease, and the startup credits that would pay for testing it.

articles.title: An open AI governance framework, and what its licence let us build
articles.teaser: Twenty open AI governance controls under CC BY-SA, why the licence matters, and the same day's conversion into a graph, a database and a walk down to EU law.

articles.title: Where is the why? A permission prompt asked me to decide, and kept the reason
articles.teaser: A prompt asked for a decision and kept the reason. Read through the policy, the law on uninformed consent, and the fixes that worked: put the why in the prompt.

articles.title: The Mandate Stack: a multi-agent system in production, layer by layer
articles.teaser: A multi-agent system that runs a business every few hours: eight layers, one written mandate per agent, everything a graph, one human who sends.

articles.title: Why my agents do not run on my laptop: chat, Cowork and Code in the cloud, a vault as the shared drive, and the two walls an operating system has
articles.teaser: An OS has two hard walls, the kernel and the user; an agent on a laptop runs inside the one marked you, so the agents run in the cloud with a vault as shared drive.

articles.title: The deck I could not download: an author-first home for presentations, as a business plan somebody else can build
articles.teaser: One download offered as a subscription, an author paid nothing, and a design for the service the author would have chosen: vaults, keys, seven roles, 85% to the author.

articles.title: The agent team as it runs: one person, twelve agents, encrypted vaults, and a mailbox nobody sends from
articles.teaser: Twelve agents on dedicated accounts, encrypted vaults as the only memory, messages as files, a folder per person, and a mailbox nobody sends from.

articles.title: A personal agent that keeps your secrets: the 2026 agents read through behaviour policy and encryption, and a privacy-first design on vaults, enclaves and the browser
articles.teaser: The 2026 personal agents read through behaviour policy and encryption, and a design on vaults, an attested enclave and the browser where no vendor holds a key.

articles.title: The investigation GitHub owes its customers: why a global outage of a platform the world deploys through deserves an aviation-style inquiry, and how the evidence could now be gathered
articles.teaser: A global GitHub Actions outage read the way aviation reads an incident: independent inquiry, near-miss reporting, second and third stories, vaults for the evidence.

articles.title: Send an agent, not a spreadsheet: the next generation of software due diligence, and why the companies that stopped reading their code are about to be asked about it
articles.teaser: Due diligence never scaled because it was a form; a buyer can now send an agent into a vendor's environment and read what the code and the practices are.

articles.title: How much of this did I write? The numbers behind twenty articles in four weeks, and what the input actually was
articles.teaser: Twenty articles in four weeks, measured from the session record: 63,000 words in, 85,000 out, no one-line prompts, and the real input is twenty years of writing.

articles.title: If somebody built a company on code review: how I would do it, and why it is only now possible
articles.teaser: A reader's seven questions answered as a company plan: one reader for every layer, review as a science, and the layers as the customer's own.

articles.title: The identity we wanted to give the agents: a week of design, the line in Google's terms, and why login plus secrets is still too hard
articles.teaser: A week of designing identities for agents and users met Google's terms; what survived is a passkey-unlocked keyring and a gap nobody sells.

articles.title: The wall under the reply: end an email with the state of the thread, not the thread
articles.teaser: End an email reply with the state of the thread for this reader, not the quoted wall: decided, open, next, who is on copy, with links to the record.

articles.title: Memory is not a spectator sport: how a web of open sites, graphs and vaults became the memory for sessions like this one
articles.teaser: Agentic memory as context management: many published, fractal, provenance-carrying memories rather than one store, shown in the session that wrote the article.

articles.title: Code review as a fractal semantic graph: source code is already one, and the review should read every layer of it
articles.teaser: Source code is layers within layers, each a graph with its own vocabulary; code review should read a change at every one, and a vault shows it done on real code.

articles.title: Replicating the agentic inbox: a walkthrough from one Claude session to a team of agents that never press send
articles.teaser: How to copy a working agentic email setup in phases: a mailbox and Claude seat of the agent's own, one session with a policy, then roles talking in files.

articles.title: Price it, then give it away: the early access programme as the next step after "do they miss it"
articles.teaser: Define the product, price it, deliver it at a cost that grows a step at a time, then offer it free to people who know you and measure what it costs them.

articles.title: Footprint and blast radius: what the agent actually did, and what it would have cost
articles.teaser: Footprint is what an agent actually did, read afterwards from logs and vault history; blast radius is what a row of its reach would cost the business today.

articles.title: Custom UIs are not the exception: the inbox in 2026, where every message has its own universe
articles.teaser: Every message has a graph, so it can be shaped for the reader's moment; a custom interface per moment is now how interfaces get made, and each gets a policy.

articles.title: The ultimate insider: agents, the infrastructure that cannot hold them, and risk management that cannot keep up
articles.teaser: Agents, the infrastructure meant to contain them, and risk management run on spreadsheets are arriving at once, and together they are one scenario.

articles.title: The reader was always the product: a corrected history of how news got into this mess
articles.teaser: News has sold the reader to advertisers since 1833; the web took the monopoly, the platforms made the reader measurable, and AI took the traffic.

articles.title: Six agents, one inbox: what a real multi-agent setup taught me about access policies
articles.teaser: An access policy for an agent is only as real as its worst row: every rule in a real six-agent setup, graded by how it is enforced today.

articles.title: Sixteen thousand fetches, ten clicks, and a token bill nobody is sending: the case for paying publishers to be easy to read
articles.teaser: AI answer engines pay to read the web as HTML; a publisher who serves markdown, dates, hashes and a typed graph saves them tokens and should get a share.

articles.title: A supply chain of vaults: how GenAI, open data and small custom tools could bring the price of food down
articles.teaser: The food chain is a data problem: one encrypted vault per party, joined by append lanes and a typed graph, could cut the waste that keeps prices high.

articles.title: Every risk is already accepted. The only question is by whom, and for how long.
articles.teaser: A risk exists the moment the exposure does, so somebody is already carrying it; the only questions worth asking are who has accepted it and until when.

articles.title: Before you give an agent a connector, give the connector a twin
articles.teaser: An agent with a Gmail or Calendar connector can do things the platform cannot undo; a journal of every call, replayed, shows what it did and what can go back.

articles.title: The future of news is the story vault, not the paywall
articles.teaser: A story is a graph of claims and evidence and the article is one projection of it; keep the graph in a vault and sell what the article was made from.

articles.title: For a startup, the most important question is whether they miss it
articles.teaser: Ship something usable, give it away briefly, take it away and see whether anybody misses it; charge at a profit before you talk to investors.

articles.title: The SaaS apocalypse will be decided by inertia, not by AI
articles.teaser: Incumbents and newcomers have the same AI; what separates them is how much past success each has to protect, so inertia decides which SaaS companies survive.

articles.title: Fractal Semantic Graphs: everything connects to everything, and nobody has to share a schema
articles.teaser: A fractal semantic graph has no privileged level and no single schema: each world keeps its own vocabulary and connects to others through named edges.

articles.title: The proof moved up, the homepage after the rebuild, next to the before pictures
articles.teaser: The rebuilt homepage puts four real vaults under one sentence, picks six by the job they do, and computes its numbers at build time from the site's own data.

articles.title: The proof is two clicks behind the claim, what the homepage gets wrong, and the fix
articles.teaser: The homepage leads with encryption, which cannot be seen, while twenty-five vaults a stranger can open in one click sit two clicks away in a table.

articles.title: A chat box on a site with no server, the plan, and the trade it makes
articles.teaser: sgit.ai has no server, so its directory chat runs a local matcher by default, takes your own key as an opt-in, and leaves the vault bridge unbuilt.

articles.title: Twenty sites in fifteen days, and what that did to the writing
articles.teaser: One site became twenty repositories in fifteen days because each argument needed its own version history, and the index now starts from a question.

articles.title: Git for things you cannot put on GitHub
articles.teaser: sgit is git for files you cannot put on GitHub: encrypted before they leave your machine, versioned like git, stored where the server cannot read a byte.

articles.title: Seven vaults, one method
articles.teaser: Publishing seven encrypted vaults in a fortnight produced a method, and every rule in it exists because something went wrong first.

articles.title: Green does not mean live
articles.teaser: Two releases passed every check and never reached the site because the checks stopped at the git remote; a release now ends by asking the live site its version.
